result.summary: The hymn opens by praising Poseidon as shaker of the earth and lord of the sea, Helicon and Aegae. It names his two offices, tamer of horses and saviour of ships, and ends with a prayer for kindness to sailors.

scenes.title: Hymn of praise to Poseidon
scenes.summary: The singer announces a song for Poseidon, names his domains and honours, and asks him to help sailors.
scenes.stakes: Sailors at sea depend on the god's favour for safe voyages.

characters.name: Poseidon
characters.description: great god of the sea and earthquakes, tamer of horses and saviour of ships

alias_notes.explanation: An epithet for Poseidon as the god of earthquakes; 'Holder of the Earth' is a similar title.

notable_quotes.reason: Concisely states Poseidon's two roles: tamer of horses and saviour of ships.

analysis.text: The hymn defines Poseidon by his two powers, horses and ships, and asks for his protection of sailors. This is the typical Homeric Hymn pattern of invocation, praise and prayer.
Such short hymns served as preludes to recitations at festivals and contests. Sailing was dangerous, so sea gods were honoured with prayers for safe passage.

fun_facts.text: Helicon, named here as Poseidon's, is better known as the mountain of the Muses in Boeotia.

language_notes.text: "Fruitless sea" is a stock phrase: the sea yields no crops, unlike farmland.
Aegae was a cult-centre of Poseidon; its exact location is uncertain, and the hymn pairs it with Helicon as places of his worship.
"Two-fold office" means two functions or privileges, assigned to Poseidon by the gods' division of powers.
"Hail" is a formal greeting of farewell and salutation that traditionally closes a Homeric Hymn.

context_notes.text: Helicon is a mountain in Boeotia, best known as sacred to the Muses, but Poseidon was also worshipped there.
Poseidon was linked with horses, and was credited with creating the first horse; he was also the god sailors prayed to for safe voyages.

literary_notes.text: The singer turns from describing the god to addressing him directly, making the hymn a prayer.
Titles such as "Holder of the Earth" and "dark-haired lord" are traditional descriptive names that identify and honour the god.
